claim: Gm7068 (CatSpere) and Tex40 (CatSperz) genes encode novel subunits of a 9-subunit CatSper ion channel complex
source: We report that the Gm7068 (CatSpere) and Tex40 (CatSperz) genes encode novel subunits of a 9-subunit CatSper ion channel complex.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 including co-immunoprecipitation and localization studies.

claim: Targeted disruption of CatSperz reduces CatSper current in mice
source: Targeted disruption of CatSperz reduces CatSper current and sperm rheotactic efficiency in mice, resulting in severe male subfertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3, demonstrating reduced ICatSper in CatSperz-null spermatozoa (~60% of normal).

claim: Targeted disruption of CatSperz reduces sperm rheotactic efficiency in mice
source: Targeted disruption of CatSperz reduces CatSper current and sperm rheotactic efficiency in mice, resulting in severe male subfertility.
evidence: This is supported by rheotaxis experiments shown in Figure 6A-B demonstrating significantly reduced rheotactic ability of CatSperz-null spermatozoa.

claim: Targeted disruption of CatSperz results in severe male subfertility
source: Targeted disruption of CatSperz reduces CatSper current and sperm rheotactic efficiency in mice, resulting in severe male subfertility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fertility tests shown in Figure 2A-B, where CatSperz-null males showed 20% complete infertility and significantly reduced litter sizes.

claim: The CatSper complex lacking CatSperζ is disrupted at ~0.8 μm intervals along the flagellum
source: Normally distributed in linear quadrilateral nanodomains along the flagellum, the complex lacking CatSperζ is disrupted at ~0.8 μm intervals along the flagellum.
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, showing periodic disruptions with autocorrelation analysis revealing ~850 nm periodicity and Fourier transform showing fundamental frequency of (800 nm)−1.

claim: Disruption of CatSperζ renders the proximal flagellum inflexible
source: This disruption renders the proximal flagellum inflexible and alters the 3D flagellar envelope, thus preventing sperm from reorienting against fluid flow in vitro and efficiently migrating in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flagellar waveform analysis in Figure 2F and Videos 2-3, showing rigidity from midpiece to midway through the principal piece.

claim: Disruption of CatSperζ alters the 3D flagellar envelope
source: This disruption renders the proximal flagellum inflexible and alters the 3D flagellar envelope, thus preventing sperm from reorienting against fluid flow in vitro and efficiently migrating in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by swimming trajectory analysis in Figure 2E and Figure 6C, and the working model in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing constrained flagellar envelope.

claim: Disruption of CatSperζ prevents sperm from reorienting against fluid flow in vitro
source: This disruption renders the proximal flagellum inflexible and alters the 3D flagellar envelope, thus preventing sperm from reorienting against fluid flow in vitro and efficiently migrating in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in-capillary rheotaxis experiments in Figure 6A-B and Video 4, showing that most CatSperz-null spermatozoa were unable to reorient and swim against flow.

claim: Disruption of CatSperζ prevents sperm from efficiently migrating in vivo
source: This disruption renders the proximal flagellum inflexible and alters the 3D flagellar envelope, thus preventing sperm from reorienting against fluid flow in vitro and efficiently migrating in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo migration data in Figure 2C showing no sperm found in COCs at 8 hr after coitus with CatSperz-null males, and delayed fertilization rates in Figure 2D.

claim: Ejaculated CatSperz-null sperm cells retrieved from the mated female uterus partially rescue in vitro fertilization that failed with epididymal spermatozoa alone
source: Ejaculated CatSperz-null sperm cells retrieved from the mated female uterus partially rescue in vitro fertilization (IVF) that failed with epididymal spermatozoa alone.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVF experiments in Figure 6E showing that ejaculated CatSperz-null sperm achieved 20% fertilization rate compared to 0.7% with epididymal sperm.

claim: Human CatSperε is quadrilaterally arranged along the flagella
source: Human CatSperε is quadrilaterally arranged along the flagella, similar to the CatSper complex in mouse sperm.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D STORM imaging in Figure 1J showing the four-fold arrangement of human CatSperε.

claim: Human CatSperε arrangement is similar to the CatSper complex in mouse sperm
source: Human CatSperε is quadrilaterally arranged along the flagella, similar to the CatSper complex in mouse sperm.
evidence: This is supported by comparing 3D STORM images of human CatSperε (Figure 1J) with mouse CatSperζ (Figure 1I), both showing quadrilateral arrangement.

claim: CatSperζ is a late evolutionary adaptation to maximize fertilization inside the mammalian female reproductive tract
source: We speculate that the newly identified CatSperζ subunit is a late evolutionary adaptation to maximize fertilization inside the mammalian female reproductive tract.
evidence: This speculation is based on evolutionary analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A showing CatSperζ is only present in mammals, unlike other CatSper subunits with more ancient origins.

claim: Sperm hyperactivation is characterized by a large asymmetric lateral displacement of the flagellum
source: Sperm hyperactivation, characterized by a large asymmetric lateral displacement of the flagellum (Ishijima et al., 2002), is required for normal mammalian sperm navigation (Demott and Suarez, 1992), rheotaxis (Miki and Clapham, 2013), and zona pellucida (ZP) penetration (Stauss et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Ishijima et al., 2002).

claim: Sperm hyperactivation is required for normal mammalian sperm navigation
source: Sperm hyperactivation, characterized by a large asymmetric lateral displacement of the flagellum (Ishijima et al., 2002), is required for normal mammalian sperm navigation (Demott and Suarez, 1992), rheotaxis (Miki and Clapham, 2013), and zona pellucida (ZP) penetration (Stauss et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Demott and Suarez, 1992.

claim: Sperm hyperactivation is required for rheotaxis
source: Sperm hyperactivation, characterized by a large asymmetric lateral displacement of the flagellum (Ishijima et al., 2002), is required for normal mammalian sperm navigation (Demott and Suarez, 1992), rheotaxis (Miki and Clapham, 2013), and zona pellucida (ZP) penetration (Stauss et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miki and Clapham, 2013.

claim: Sperm hyperactivation is required for zona pellucida penetration
source: Sperm hyperactivation, characterized by a large asymmetric lateral displacement of the flagellum (Ishijima et al., 2002), is required for normal mammalian sperm navigation (Demott and Suarez, 1992), rheotaxis (Miki and Clapham, 2013), and zona pellucida (ZP) penetration (Stauss et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stauss et al., 1995.

claim: Calcium influx through the flagellar Ca2+ ion channel CatSper triggers hyperactivation
source: Calcium influx through the flagellar Ca2+ ion channel, CatSper, triggers hyperactivation (Carlson et al., 2003; Kirichok et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2001) and leads to changes in the flagellar envelope during capacitation (Chung et al., 2011; Quill et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carlson et al., 2003; Kirichok et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2001.

claim: Calcium influx through CatSper leads to changes in the flagellar envelope during capacitation
source: Calcium influx through the flagellar Ca2+ ion channel, CatSper, triggers hyperactivation (Carlson et al., 2003; Kirichok et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2001) and leads to changes in the flagellar envelope during capacitation (Chung et al., 2011; Quill et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2011; Quill et al., 2003.

claim: In hyperactivated spermatozoa, the transverse flagellar force is larger than the propulsive flagellar force due to the increase in mid-piece curvature
source: In hyperactivated spermatozoa, the transverse flagellar force is larger than the propulsive flagellar force due to the increase in mid-piece curvature (α angle), which enables a larger range of motion and typical figure-of-eight swimming trajectories compared to the nearly straight paths of non-hyperactivated spermatozoa (Ishijima, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ishijima, 2011.

claim: Increased mid-piece curvature enables a larger range of motion and typical figure-of-eight swimming trajectories compared to the nearly straight paths of non-hyperactivated spermatozoa
source: In hyperactivated spermatozoa, the transverse flagellar force is larger than the propulsive flagellar force due to the increase in mid-piece curvature (α angle), which enables a larger range of motion and typical figure-of-eight swimming trajectories compared to the nearly straight paths of non-hyperactivated spermatozoa (Ishijima, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ishijima, 2011.

claim: Transverse force facilitates sperm penetration through the cumulus and zona pellucida
source: Transverse force facilitates sperm penetration through the cumulus and ZP (Ishijima, 2011; Yanagimachi, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ishijima, 2011; Yanagimachi, 1966.

claim: Spermatozoa from all CatSper-null (1–4 or d) males have smaller α angles than wild-type spermatozoa upon capacitation
source: Spermatozoa from all CatSper-null (1–4 or d) males have smaller α angles than wild-type (wt spermatozoa upon capacitation (Chung et al., 2011; Qi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2011; Qi et al., 2007.

claim: CatSper-null mutant spermatozoa migrate inefficiently in vivo
source: Consistently, CatSper-null mutant spermatozoa migrate inefficiently in vivo (Chung et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2009) and fail to penetrate the ZP (Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2009.

claim: CatSper-null mutant spermatozoa fail to penetrate the zona pellucida
source: Consistently, CatSper-null mutant spermatozoa migrate inefficiently in vivo (Chung et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2009) and fail to penetrate the ZP (Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ren et al., 2001.

claim: Sperm rheotax against Fallopian tubular and isthmus fluid flow
source: Sperm rheotax against Fallopian tubular and isthmus fluid flow (Miki and Clapham, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miki and Clapham, 2013.

claim: Rheotactic turning to reorient to directional flow depends on flagellar rolling, not the sperm head or its geometry
source: Rheotactic turning to reorient to directional flow depends on flagellar rolling, not the sperm head or its geometry, as demonstrated by the rheotaxis of headless mouse sperm (Miki and Clapham, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miki and Clapham, 2013, which demonstrated rheotaxis of headless mouse sperm.

claim: CatSper channels form unique Ca2+ signaling domains in linearly quadrilateral arrays along the principal piece of sperm flagella
source: CatSper channels form unique Ca2+ signaling domains in linearly quadrilateral arrays along the principal piece of sperm flagella.
evidence: This is supported by 3D STORM imaging data in Figure 1I-J and Figure 5C showing the quadrilateral arrangement.

claim: The integrity of CatSper Ca2+ signaling domains is necessary to time and/or maintain hyperactivated motility
source: The integrity of these domains is necessary to time and/or maintain hyperactivated motility (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: CatSper1-null sperm cannot rheotax due to defects in rolling
source: Thus, CatSper1-null sperm cannot rheotax due to defects in rolling (Miki and Clapham, 2013), and presumably exert less lateral force in escaping from epithelial walls (Ho et al., 2009) or in pushing cumulus cells aside.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miki and Clapham, 2013.

claim: CatSper1-null sperm presumably exert less lateral force in escaping from epithelial walls
source: Thus, CatSper1-null sperm cannot rheotax due to defects in rolling (Miki and Clapham, 2013), and presumably exert less lateral force in escaping from epithelial walls (Ho et al., 2009) or in pushing cumulus cells aside.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ho et al., 2009 and uses the qualifier 'presumably' indicating inference.

claim: CatSperε has the same ancient origin at the root of early eukaryotic evolution as CatSpers1-4, b, and g
source: CatSpere has the same ancient origin at the root of early eukaryotic evolution as those of CatSpers1-4, b, and g and the same pattern of extensive lineage-specific gene loss as CatSperb and g through metazoan evolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citation to Cai et al., 2014.

claim: CatSperε has the same pattern of extensive lineage-specific gene loss as CatSperb and g through metazoan evolution
source: CatSpere has the same ancient origin at the root of early eukaryotic evolution as those of CatSpers1-4, b, and g and the same pattern of extensive lineage-specific gene loss as CatSperb and g through metazoan evolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citation to Cai et al., 2014.

claim: CatSperδ appears later in evolution than CatSperε
source: While CatSper δ and ε share high C-terminal sequence homology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), CatSperδ appears later in evolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by evolutionary analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A showing CatSperδ distribution across species.

claim: CatSperζ is only present in mammals
source: In contrast, CatSperζ has no conserved domains and, like hyperactivated motility, is only present in mammals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), leading us to speculate that CatSperζ is a required evolutionary adaptation to mammalian fertilization.
evidence: This is supported by evolutionary analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A showing CatSperζ distribution only in mammals.

claim: Hyperactivated motility is only present in mammals
source: In contrast, CatSperζ has no conserved domains and, like hyperactivated motility, is only present in mammals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), leading us to speculate that CatSperζ is a required evolutionary adaptation to mammalian fertilization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the context of comparing CatSperζ evolution.

claim: CatSperz-null mutant mice are indistinguishable from their wt or heterozygous littermates in appearance, gross behavior, or survival
source: CatSperz-null mutant mice are indistinguishable from their wt or heterozygous (het) littermates in appearance, gross behavior, or survival.
evidence: This is an observational statement about the phenotype of the knockout mice.

claim: No morphological differences were observed by histological examination of testis and epididymis in CatSperz-null mice
source: In addition, no morphological differences were observed by histological examination of testis and epididymis (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from histological examination.

claim: Sperm morphology from CatSperz-null mice was not significantly different from heterozygous littermates
source: Sperm morphology and epididymal sperm number from CatSperz-null mice were not significantly different from those of 2–3 month old paired heterozygous littermates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Epididymal sperm number from CatSperz-null mice was not significantly different from heterozygous littermates
source: Sperm morphology and epididymal sperm number from CatSperz-null mice were not significantly different from those of 2–3 month old paired heterozygous littermates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A showing similar sperm counts.

claim: CatSperz-null female mice exhibited normal mating behavior
source: CatSperz-null female mice exhibited normal mating behavior and gave birth to litters comparable to those of het females when mated with wt or het males (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fertility data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: CatSperz-null female mice gave birth to litters comparable to heterozygous females when mated with wt or het males
source: CatSperz-null female mice exhibited normal mating behavior and gave birth to litters comparable to those of het females when mated with wt or het males (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fertility data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 20% of CatSperz-null males were completely infertile over six months
source: However, when CatSperz-null male mice were mated with wt or het females, they were severely subfertile: 20% (5/25) CatSperz-null males were completely infertile over six months (Figure 2A), and progeny of the fertile paternal CatSperz-null mice were significantly fewer in number (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fertility test data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Progeny of fertile paternal CatSperz-null mice were significantly fewer in number
source: However, when CatSperz-null male mice were mated with wt or het females, they were severely subfertile: 20% (5/25) CatSperz-null males were completely infertile over six months (Figure 2A), and progeny of the fertile paternal CatSperz-null mice were significantly fewer in number (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by litter size data in Figure 2B showing average litter size of 4.4 for CatSperz-null vs 7.4 for heterozygous.

claim: The latency from pair formation to birth of offspring from CatSperz-null males was ≥10 days compared to wt or het males
source: The latency from pair formation to the birth of these offspring from CatSperz-null males was ≥10 days compared to those from wt or het males (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from breeding experiments.

claim: No sperm was found in cumulus oocyte complexes at 8 hr after coitus when mated with CatSperz-null male mice
source: At 8 hr after coitus, no sperm was found in the COCs when mated with CatSperz-null male mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by sperm migration data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The majority of cumulus oocyte complexes from CatSperz-het mated females had one or more sperm cells within the complex at 8 hr after coitus
source: In contrast, the majority of the COCs from CatSperz-het mated females had one or more sperm cells within the complex.
evidence: This is supported by sperm migration data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When mated with CatSperz-het males, more 2 cell eggs were observed over time after coitus
source: When mated with CatSperz-het males, more 2 cell eggs were observed over time after coitus, while the fertilization rate by CatSperz-null males did not change significantly (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo fertilization rate data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The fertilization rate by CatSperz-null males did not change significantly over time after coitus
source: When mated with CatSperz-het males, more 2 cell eggs were observed over time after coitus, while the fertilization rate by CatSperz-null males did not change significantly (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo fertilization rate data in Figure 2D showing similar rates at 20 hr (21.3%) and 27-30 hr (24.6%).

claim: CatSperz-null spermatozoa did not show the characteristic increase of lateral head displacement upon capacitation
source: However, the characteristic increase of lateral head displacement upon capacitation was not observed in z-null spermatozoa (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that hyperactivated motility was reduced.
evidence: This is supported by CASA data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D showing no significant change in ALH for CatSperz-null sperm.

claim: CatSperz-null spermatozoa have reduced hyperactivated motility
source: However, the characteristic increase of lateral head displacement upon capacitation was not observed in z-null spermatozoa (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that hyperactivated motility was reduced.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increase in lateral head displacement and supported by swimming trajectory data in Figure 2E.

claim: CatSperz-null spermatozoa remain bent in the anti-hook direction
source: Moreover, CatSperz-null spermatozoa remain bent in the anti-hook direction (Ishijima et al., 2002) (Figure 2F, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flagellar waveform analysis in Figure 2F and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: The anti-hook bend predominates as the pro-hook bend is dysregulated in CatSperz-null spermatozoa
source: The anti-hook bend predominates as the pro-hook bend (initiated by the CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling pathway (Chang and Suarez, 2011) is dysregulated in CatSperz-null spermatozoa.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CatSperz-null sperm remain bent in anti-hook direction and supported by citation to Chang and Suarez, 2011.

claim: Pro-hook bend is initiated by the CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling pathway
source: The anti-hook bend predominates as the pro-hook bend (initiated by the CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling pathway (Chang and Suarez, 2011) is dysregulated in CatSperz-null spermatozoa.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang and Suarez, 2011.

claim: In CatSperz-null spermatozoa, monovalent CatSper current is reduced to ~60% of normal
source: However, in CatSperz-null spermatozoa, monovalent CatSper current is present but reduced to ~60% of normal (−426 ± 50 pA at −100 mV; Figure 3A) compared to control CatSperz-het spermatozoa (−683 ± 77 pA at −100 mV; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: In the absence of CatSperζ, the CatSper channel complex is still targeted to the flagellar membrane and forms functional channels
source: Thus, in the absence of CatSperζ, the CatSper channel complex is still targeted to the flagellar membrane and forms functional channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of reduced but functional ICatSper in CatSperz-null spermatozoa shown in Figure 3.

claim: The reduction in CatSper current reflects decreased protein expression levels
source: We hypothesize that the reduction in CatSper current reflected decreased protein expression levels.
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A-B showing 30-60% reduction in CatSper subunit expression.

claim: ATP-activated cation-nonselective current in the midpiece of murine sperm is mediated by the P2X2 purinergic receptor
source: P2X receptors are nonselective ion channels gated by purines such as ATP. The ATP-activated cation-nonselective current in the midpiece of murine sperm is mediated by the P2X2 purinergic receptor (Navarro et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Navarro et al., 2011.

claim: In CatSperz-null spermatozoa, IATP did not differ substantially from heterozygous spermatozoa
source: In CatSperz-null spermatozoa, IATP did not differ substantially from heterozygous spermatozoa (Figure 3A and B), supporting the assumption that there is selective down regulation of CatSper channels.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 3A and B showing similar IATP in both genotypes.

claim: Protein tyrosine phosphorylation is a hallmark of sperm capacitation
source: Protein tyrosine phosphorylation (P-Tyr), a hallmark of sperm capacitation, is potentiated and delocalized in CatSper knockout mice (Chung et al., 2014) or when Ca2+ influx is pharmacologically blocked (Navarrete et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Protein tyrosine phosphorylation is potentiated and delocalized in CatSper knockout mice
source: Protein tyrosine phosphorylation (P-Tyr), a hallmark of sperm capacitation, is potentiated and delocalized in CatSper knockout mice (Chung et al., 2014) or when Ca2+ influx is pharmacologically blocked (Navarrete et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2014 and Navarrete et al., 2015.

claim: Upon capacitation, P-Tyr was more prominent in CatSperz-null spermatozoa than wt, but to a lesser extent than CatSper1-null spermatozoa
source: Upon capacitation, P-Tyr was more prominent in CatSperz-null spermatozoa than wt, but to a lesser extent than CatSper1-null spermatozoa (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), consistent with the reduced calcium current.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E showing P-Tyr levels.

claim: Other CatSper subunits are completely absent in CatSper1- and CatSperd-null spermatozoa
source: This contrasts with the complete absence of other CatSper subunits in CatSper1- and CatSperd-null spermatozoa.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A showing no CatSper subunit expression in CatSper1 and d-null sperm.

claim: mRNA and protein levels of other CatSper subunits were not reduced in the testis of CatSperz-null mice
source: mRNA and protein levels of other CatSper subunits were not reduced in the testis of CatSperz-null mice (Figure 4C and D), suggesting that the defect occurs during or after assembly of the protein complex.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4D.

claim: The defect in CatSper expression in CatSperz-null spermatozoa occurs during or after assembly of the protein complex
source: mRNA and protein levels of other CatSper subunits were not reduced in the testis of CatSperz-null mice (Figure 4C and D), suggesting that the defect occurs during or after assembly of the protein complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mRNA and protein levels are normal in testis but reduced in mature sperm.

claim: Loss of CatSperz resulted in fragmentation of CatSper1 staining on the flagellar membrane
source: Loss of CatSperz resulted in fragmentation of CatSper1 staining on the flagellar membrane and these defects are large enough to be resolved by confocal imaging (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 5A showing gaps in CatSper1 staining.

claim: Gaps in CatSper staining were not observed in wt/het or previous wt and CatSper knockout studies
source: These gaps were not observed in wt/het (Figure 1H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) or previous wt and CatSper knockout studies (Chung et al., 2011; 2014; Liu et al., 2007; Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with images in Figure 1H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, and citations to previous studies.

claim: In CatSperz-null spermatozoa, each 'stripe' of the CatSper domains is fragmented while the overall quadrilateral structure is maintained
source: 3D STED and 3D STORM super-resolution microscopies clearly demonstrate that structural continuity is interrupted in CatSperz-null spermatozoa - each 'stripe' of the CatSper domains is fragmented, while the overall quadrilateral structure is maintained (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The distance between ribs of the fibrous sheath is about 800 nm in mouse spermatozoa
source: Based on scanning electron micrographs (Danshina et al., 2010; Miki et al., 2004), we find that the distance between ribs is about 800 nm in mouse spermatozoa.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published scanning electron micrographs cited from Danshina et al., 2010; Miki et al., 2004.

claim: The repeated disruption in the absence of CatSperζ is likely related to rib spacing of the fibrous sheath
source: Thus, it seems likely that the repeated disruption in the absence of CatSperz is related to rib spacing of the FS.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between the ~800 nm periodicity of CatSper disruption and the ~800 nm rib spacing.

claim: Genetic abrogation of CatSper disrupts hyperactivated motility as manifested by changes in movement symmetry, amplitude, and rolling
source: Genetic abrogation of CatSper disrupts hyperactivated motility as manifested by changes in movement symmetry, amplitude, and rolling (Carlson et al., 2003; Chung et al., 2011; Miki and Clapham, 2013; Qi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carlson et al., 2003; Chung et al., 2011; Miki and Clapham, 2013; Qi et al., 2007.

claim: PP2B-Aγ expresses throughout the tail but is localized to the CatSper quadrilateral structures and axoneme
source: We previously reported that the catalytic subunit of calcineurin, PP2B-Aγ, expresses throughout the tail but localized to the CatSper quadrilateral structures and axoneme (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: In CatSper1-null spermatozoa, PP2B-Aγ remains localized primarily to the axoneme but disappears from the quadrilateral structures
source: In CatSper1-null spermatozoa, PP2B-Aγ remains localized primarily to the axoneme but disappears from the quadrilateral structures.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' work.

claim: A similar but not identical phenotype (inflexible midpiece, reduced hyperactivated motility, and impaired ZP penetration) was reported in testis-specific calcineurin Ppp3cc-null and Ppp3r2-null spermatozoa
source: Recently, a similar but not identical phenotype (inflexible midpiece, reduced hyperactivated motility, and impaired ZP penetration) was reported in testis-specific calcineurin Ppp3cc-null and Ppp3r2-null spermatozoa (Miyata et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miyata et al., 2015.

claim: The principal piece of both CatSper1-null and Ppp3cc-null spermatozoa are not rigid
source: Note that the principal piece of both CatSper1-null and Ppp3cc-null spermatozoa are not rigid.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to distinguish the CatSperz-null phenotype.

claim: Inflexibility in the proximal regions of flagellum results in a flagellar envelope approximated as a rod with a distal propeller
source: In any case, inflexibility in the proximal regions of flagellum results in a flagellar envelope approximated as a rod with a distal propeller.
evidence: This is a conceptual model inferred from the observed rigidity and movement patterns.

claim: The smaller lateral deviation in CatSperz-null sperm reduces torque
source: The sperm can rotate faster but the smaller lateral deviation reduces torque.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of faster rotation (Figure 6D) but reduced rheotactic ability (Figure 6A-B).

claim: Reduced torque limits the sperm's ability to orient into the flow
source: This limits the sperm's ability to orient into the flow, as well as penetrate the cumulus and ZP.
evidence: This is inferred from the rheotaxis and IVF data in Figure 6.

claim: Reduced torque limits the sperm's ability to penetrate the cumulus and zona pellucida
source: This limits the sperm's ability to orient into the flow, as well as penetrate the cumulus and ZP.
evidence: This is inferred from IVF data in Figure 6E-F showing failure to fertilize cumulus-intact oocytes.

claim: Epididymal sperm are commonly used in genetically tractable mouse studies
source: While ejaculated sperm are preferred for fertilization studies in larger animals and humans, epididymal sperm are commonly used in genetically tractable mouse studies.
evidence: This is stated as common practice in the field.

claim: Epididymal sperm are not exposed to accessory sex gland secretions and female fluids
source: Notably, these sperm are not exposed to accessory sex gland secretions and female fluids.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the difference between epididymal and ejaculated sperm.

claim: Natural modulators absent in epididymal sperm IVF studies may partially rescue the fertilizing potential of CatSperz-null spermatozoa by activating Ca2+ signaling activity
source: Perhaps natural modulators, absent in epididymal sperm IVF studies, partially rescue the fertilizing potential of CatSperz-null spermatozoa by activating Ca2+ signaling activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that ejaculated CatSperz-null sperm perform better in IVF than epididymal sperm (Figure 6E).

claim: A transient pulse of Ca2+ can greatly reduce the capacitation time required for wt sperm to develop hyperactivated motility
source: Interestingly, a transient pulse of Ca2+ can greatly reduce the capacitation time required for wt sperm to develop hyperactivated motility (Tateno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tateno et al., 2013.

claim: A short exposure to A23187 rescued the defects in motility and fertilizing capability of CatSper1-null sperm in vitro
source: Moreover, Navarrete et al recently demonstrated that a short exposure to A23187 rescued the defects in motility and fertilizing capability of CatSper1-null sperm in vitro (Navarrete et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Navarrete et al., 2016.

claim: The initial priming by Ca2+ influx above a certain threshold is essential for sperm function
source: These independent studies were interpreted to mean that the initial priming by Ca2+ influx, perhaps above a certain threshold, is essential for sperm function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of cited studies by Tateno et al., 2013 and Navarrete et al., 2016.

claim: The linear quadrilateral CatSper complexes are not present in CatSper1-null spermatozoa
source: However, the linear quadrilateral CatSper complexes are not present in CatSper1-null spermatozoa and in CatSperz-null spermatozoa are disrupted by gaps.
evidence: This is based on previous studies and the current super-resolution imaging data in Figure 5.

claim: The linear quadrilateral structure in vivo likely maintains, regulates, and distributes CatSper Ca2+ signaling during hyperactivated motility
source: We hypothesize that the linear quadrilateral structure in vivo likely maintains, regulates, and distributes CatSper Ca2+ signaling during hyperactivated motility.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed structural organization and functional deficits when disrupted.

claim: In vivo sperm swimming trajectories are modulated by switching between pro- and anti-hook beating patterns
source: This complexity is illustrated in vivo sperm swimming trajectories, which are modulated by switching between pro- and anti-hook beating patterns.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about sperm motility patterns.

claim: In the absence of CatSperζ, anti-hook beating predominates
source: In the absence of CatSperζ, anti-hook beating predominates.
evidence: This is supported by flagellar waveform analysis in Figure 2F and Videos 2-3.

claim: Pro-hook motions are associated with intact CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling pathways
source: Pro-hook motions are associated with intact CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling pathways (Chang and Suarez, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang and Suarez, 2011.

claim: Ejaculated sperm display more pro-hook hyperactivation than epididymal sperm
source: Finally, ejaculated sperm display more pro-hook hyperactivation than epididymal sperm (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2015.

claim: CatSper's unique composition and central role in hyperactivated motility make it an ideal target for contraception
source: CatSper's unique composition and central role in hyperactivated motility make it an ideal target for contraception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about CatSper's essential role in fertility.

claim: CatSperε is predicted to encode a single transmembrane protein
source: This testis-specific gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) is predicted to encode a single transmembrane (TM) protein (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C including hydrophilicity plots.

claim: CatSperε and CatSperζ are testis-specific genes
source: This testis-specific gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) is predicted to encode a single transmembrane (TM) protein (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C). In addition, a small soluble protein encoded by another testis-specific gene, Tex40 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), was found to be associated with the CatSper channel complex (Figure 1B and C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tissue expression profile in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing expression only in testis.

claim: CatSperε and CatSperζ mRNAs express specifically in germ cells
source: Like the other CatSper accessory subunits (Chung et al., 2011), both CatSpere and CatSperz mRNAs express specifically in germ cells and are detected before CatSper1 expression during postnatal development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and temporal expression analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: CatSperε and CatSperζ are detected before CatSper1 expression during postnatal development
source: Like the other CatSper accessory subunits (Chung et al., 2011), both CatSpere and CatSperz mRNAs express specifically in germ cells and are detected before CatSper1 expression during postnatal development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by temporal expression analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C showing earlier expression of CatSperε and ζ compared to CatSper1.

claim: Mouse CatSperε and ζ proteins partition into the testis microsome fraction
source: Moreover, mouse CatSper ε and ζ proteins partition into the testis microsome fraction (P) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), complex with CatSper1, and exhibit interdependence with the expression of the other CatSper subunits (Figure 1D–1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fractionation experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: CatSperε and ζ complex with CatSper1
source: Moreover, mouse CatSper ε and ζ proteins partition into the testis microsome fraction (P) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), complex with CatSper1, and exhibit interdependence with the expression of the other CatSper subunits (Figure 1D–1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 1D.

claim: CatSperε and ζ exhibit interdependence with the expression of the other CatSper subunits
source: Moreover, mouse CatSper ε and ζ proteins partition into the testis microsome fraction (P) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), complex with CatSper1, and exhibit interdependence with the expression of the other CatSper subunits (Figure 1D–1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 1E-F showing dependence of CatSperε and ζ on CatSper1.

claim: In both human and mouse sperm cells, CatSperε and ζ proteins are localized to the principal piece of the tails
source: In both human and mouse sperm cells, CatSper ε and ζ proteins are localized to the principal piece of the tails (Figure 1G and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 1G-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-G.

claim: Mouse CatSperζ shows the apparent four-fold arrangement of CatSper1, β and δ subunits in mouse spermatozoa
source: CatSperζ and CatSperε show the apparent four-fold arrangement of CatSper1, β and δ subunits in mouse (Figure 1I) and human (Figure 1J) spermatozoa.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D STORM imaging in Figure 1I.

claim: Human CatSperε shows the apparent four-fold arrangement of CatSper subunits in human spermatozoa
source: CatSperζ and CatSperε show the apparent four-fold arrangement of CatSper1, β and δ subunits in mouse (Figure 1I) and human (Figure 1J) spermatozoa.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D STORM imaging in Figure 1J.

claim: It has not been possible to express functional CatSper channels in heterologous systems
source: As the most biochemically complex ion channel known to date, it has not been possible to express functional CatSper channels in heterologous systems.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from attempts including injection of all 7 CatSper mRNAs into Xenopus oocytes.

claim: The CatSper channel is the most biochemically complex ion channel known to date
source: As the most biochemically complex ion channel known to date, it has not been possible to express functional CatSper channels in heterologous systems.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization based on the 9 subunit composition.

claim: CatSperz-null uncapacitated spermatozoa rotate ~50% faster than z-het spermatozoa
source: Indeed, uncapacitated CatSperz-null spermatozoa rotate ~50% faster than z-het spermatozoa (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rotation rate measurements in Figure 6D showing 3.8 Hz for CatSperz-null vs 2.4 Hz for het at 5 min.

claim: CatSperz-null spermatozoa have less lateral motion and are subject to less torque by the moving stream
source: This indicates that CatSperz-null spermatozoa have less lateral motion and are subject to less torque by the moving stream.
evidence: This is inferred from the faster rotation but reduced rheotactic ability shown in Figure 6.

claim: The rigidity of the CatSperz-null sperm proximal tail constrains its motion to that of a propeller-driven rod
source: In short, the rigidity of the CatSperz-null sperm proximal tail constrains its motion to that of a propeller-driven rod.
evidence: This is a conceptual summary inferred from the observed rigidity and movement patterns.

claim: After incubation with two-fold greater extracellular Ca2+, most CatSperz-null sperm remain bent in the anti-hook orientation with a rigid proximal tail
source: After incubation for 90 min with a two-fold greater [Ca2+], most CatSperz-null sperm remain bent in the anti-hook orientation with a rigid proximal tail (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, z(-/-) middle, and Video 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flagellar waveform analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Video 7.

claim: A few CatSperz-null spermatozoa partially recover after high Ca2+ treatment, bending occasionally in the pro-hook direction with hyperactivated motility
source: A few z-null spermatozoa partially recover, bending occasionally in the pro-hook direction with hyperactivated motility (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, z(-/-) right, and Video 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flagellar waveform analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Video 7.

claim: A 20-fold reduction of extracellular Ca2+ alone did not significantly alter the flagellar waveforms of z-het spermatozoa within 90 min
source: Conversely, a 20-fold reduction of extracellular [Ca2+] alone did not significantly alter the flagellar waveforms of z-het spermatozoa within 90 min (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Video 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flagellar waveform analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Video 8.

claim: In z-het spermatozoa, an A23187-induced Ca2+ pulse followed by washout enables full hyperactivation within 30 min
source: In z-het spermatozoa, an A23187-induced Ca2+ pulse followed by washout, enables full hyperactivation, characterized by wide lateral displacement with large midpiece α angle within 30 min (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Videos 9 and 10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flagellar waveform analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Videos 9-10.

claim: In z-null sperm, A23187 treatment improved the flexibility of the proximal flagella, particularly in the principal piece, but the midpiece remained largely inflexible
source: However, in z-null sperm, the same treatment improved the flexibility of the proximal flagella, particularly in the principal piece, but the midpiece remained largely inflexible (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Videos 9 and 10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flagellar waveform analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Videos 9-10.

claim: CatSperz-null spermatozoa cannot fertilize cumulus-intact oocytes
source: We found that these spermatozoa cannot fertilize cumulus-intact oocytes (Figure 6E), but could dissociate the cumulus cell layers and bind to the ZP (data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVF experiments in Figure 6E showing 0.7% fertilization rate with epididymal CatSperz-null sperm.

claim: CatSperz-null spermatozoa could dissociate the cumulus cell layers and bind to the zona pellucida
source: We found that these spermatozoa cannot fertilize cumulus-intact oocytes (Figure 6E), but could dissociate the cumulus cell layers and bind to the ZP (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments.

claim: Cumulus removal did not change the fertilization rate of ZP intact oocytes by CatSperz-null spermatozoa
source: Cumulus removal did not change the fertilization rate of ZP intact oocytes by CatSperz-null spermatozoa.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVF data in Figure 6F showing similar low fertilization rates with and without cumulus.

claim: The fertilization rate of CatSperz-null spermatozoa was only marginally enhanced by destabilization of the ZP by 2 mM glutathione
source: Furthermore, this rate was only marginally enhanced by destabilization of the ZP by 2 mM glutathione (Figure 6F) (Miyata et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVF data in Figure 6F showing 7% fertilization with GSH treatment.

claim: Reduced hyperactivated motility alone does not explain the failure of CatSperz-null spermatozoa in IVF
source: This indicates that reduced hyperactivated motility alone does not explain the failure of CatSperz-null spermatozoa in IVF.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that even with cumulus removal and ZP destabilization, fertilization rates remain low.

claim: The kinetics of capacitation in vitro may be different from that in vivo
source: One possibility is that the kinetics of capacitation in vitro is different from that in vivo, resulting from fluctuations in timing or amplitude of known factors (e.g., HCO3, pH) or from unknown factors present in seminal and/or female fluids.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the difference between in vitro and in vivo fertilization success.

claim: When ejaculated CatSperz-null spermatozoa flushed from the uterus were used in IVF trials, 20% of oocytes developed into two-cell embryos
source: When ejaculated spermatozoa flushed from the uterus of the mated females were used in IVF trials, 20% of oocytes incubated with z-null spermatozoa developed into two-cell embryos (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVF data in Figure 6E.

claim: Additional factors may be functionally relevant in in vivo fertilization
source: Thus, additional factors may be functionally relevant in in vivo fertilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the improved fertilization rate with ejaculated vs epididymal CatSperz-null sperm.

claim: Mouse and human CatSperε show only 50% amino acid sequence identity
source: Like many gamete-specific proteins and the other CatSper proteins reported so far (Cai and Clapham, 2008; Chung et al., 2011), mouse and human CatSper ε and ζ show signs of rapid evolutionary change with only 50% and 45% amino acid sequence identity, respectively.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: Mouse and human CatSperζ show only 45% amino acid sequence identity
source: Like many gamete-specific proteins and the other CatSper proteins reported so far (Cai and Clapham, 2008; Chung et al., 2011), mouse and human CatSper ε and ζ show signs of rapid evolutionary change with only 50% and 45% amino acid sequence identity, respectively.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: The sequence regions outside TM segments and the pore loop of CatSper proteins are poorly conserved across species
source: In particular, the sequence regions outside TM segments and the pore loop of CatSper proteins are poorly conserved across species, indicating these regions possibly convey species-specific modulation of flagellar motility (Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citation to Miller et al., 2015.

claim: There are striking differences in progesterone-elicited ICatSper responses in mouse and human
source: This is illustrated by striking differences in progesterone-elicited ICatSper responses in mouse and human (Lishko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lishko et al., 2011.

claim: The conservation pattern of the lineage-specific gain and loss of the CatSpere gene is identical to those of b and g
source: The conservation pattern of the lineage-specific gain and loss of the CatSpere gene is identical to those of b and g, suggesting that they likely belonged to an ancient CatSper channel Ca2+ signaling network before the divergence of unikonts and bikonts.
evidence: This is based on evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CatSperε, b, and g likely belonged to an ancient CatSper channel Ca2+ signaling network before the divergence of unikonts and bikonts
source: The conservation pattern of the lineage-specific gain and loss of the CatSpere gene is identical to those of b and g, suggesting that they likely belonged to an ancient CatSper channel Ca2+ signaling network before the divergence of unikonts and bikonts.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CatSper protein expression is strictly interdependent
source: Since their protein expression is strictly interdependent, we speculate that CatSpere-null mice will have the phenotype of CatSper1-4, or d-null mice.
evidence: This is based on observations from Figure 1D-F and previous studies showing interdependence.

claim: CatSperε-null mice will likely have the phenotype of CatSper1-4 or d-null mice
source: Since their protein expression is strictly interdependent, we speculate that CatSpere-null mice will have the phenotype of CatSper1-4, or d-null mice.
evidence: This is speculation based on the interdependence of CatSper subunit expression.

claim: CatSperζ may impart some adaptation as a method enabling rheotaxis in the mammalian female reproductive tract
source: In contrast, CatSperz is conserved only in mammals, suggesting that this protein imparts some adaptation, perhaps as a method enabling rheotaxis in the mammalian female reproductive tract.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mammalian-specific conservation and the rheotaxis defects observed in CatSperz-null mice.

claim: CatSperζ has no putative transmembrane domains
source: Interestingly, although CatSperζ has no putative transmembrane domains, it is localized in the same quadrilateral pattern as other CatSpers, but is not present elsewhere in sperm.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Unlike CatSper1-4 and d-null mice which produce complete infertility, CatSperz-null males exhibit an incomplete loss of fertility
source: An intriguing aspect of our observations is that, unlike CatSper1-4 and d-null mice, which produce complete infertility, CatSperz-null males exhibit an incomplete loss of fertility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fertility data in Figure 2A-B showing 80% of CatSperz-null males are fertile though with reduced litter sizes.

claim: The effects of CatSperz on channel gating remain to be determined in future studies
source: The CatSper current is reduced in CatSperz-null spermatozoa, and may have similar permeation properties (likely dominated by the CatSper1-4 pore subunits), but the effects of CatSperz on channel gating remain to be determined in future studies.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: Voltage-gated Cav channel auxiliary subunits are not required for expression but modulate expression levels and gating
source: This is reminiscent of the non-spermatozoan, voltage-gated Cav channel auxiliary subunits, which are not required for expression but modulate expression levels and gating (Catterall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Catterall et al., 2005.

claim: The fibrous sheath is a cytoskeletal structure unique to the mammalian sperm flagellum
source: The fibrous sheath (FS), a cytoskeletal structure unique to the mammalian sperm flagellum, defines the extent of the tail's principal piece, in which all the CatSper proteins are specifically localized.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about sperm structure.

claim: The fibrous sheath defines the extent of the tail's principal piece
source: The fibrous sheath (FS), a cytoskeletal structure unique to the mammalian sperm flagellum, defines the extent of the tail's principal piece, in which all the CatSper proteins are specifically localized.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about sperm structure.

claim: All CatSper proteins are specifically localized in the principal piece
source: The fibrous sheath (FS), a cytoskeletal structure unique to the mammalian sperm flagellum, defines the extent of the tail's principal piece, in which all the CatSper proteins are specifically localized.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data throughout the manuscript showing CatSper localization to the principal piece.

claim: The fibrous sheath closely lies under the plasma membrane
source: The FS closely lies under the plasma membrane and its two longitudinal columns are connected by circumferential ribs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about fibrous sheath structure.

claim: The fibrous sheath has two longitudinal columns connected by circumferential ribs
source: The FS closely lies under the plasma membrane and its two longitudinal columns are connected by circumferential ribs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about fibrous sheath structure.

claim: CatSper channels are distributed on the end of ribs where they merge with the column
source: Immunogold electron microscopy demonstrated that the CatSper channels are distributed on the end of ribs, where they merge with the column (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: The timing of occurrence and localization of CatSper Ca2+ signaling domains is likely coordinated with the assembly of fibrous sheath proteins along the axoneme
source: It seems likely that the timing of occurrence and localization of CatSper Ca2+ signaling domains is coordinated with the assembly of FS proteins along the axoneme.
evidence: This is speculation based on the correlation between CatSper localization and fibrous sheath structure.

claim: The fibrous sheath column appears early in spermiogenesis, forming from the distal tip of the tail along the axoneme
source: The column appears early in spermiogenesis, forming from the distal tip of the tail along the axoneme, followed by subsequent rib formation in the opposite direction (Oko, 1998; Oko and Clermont, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oko, 1998; Oko and Clermont, 1989.

claim: Rib formation in the fibrous sheath occurs in the opposite direction to column formation
source: The column appears early in spermiogenesis, forming from the distal tip of the tail along the axoneme, followed by subsequent rib formation in the opposite direction (Oko, 1998; Oko and Clermont, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oko, 1998; Oko and Clermont, 1989.

claim: Alterations in the CatSper structure result in changes in mechanical properties, movement of the flagellum, distribution of entering calcium, and downstream kinase activity
source: But it is important to point out that alterations in the structure should also result in changes in mechanical properties, movement of the flagellum, distribution of entering calcium, and downstream kinase activity and the motor elements they regulate.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of structural disruption.
